ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: This study was approved by the 15 Research Ethics Committee of Morinomiya University of Medical Sciences (Approval Number: 2024-032).

When interpreting the absence of immediate improvements in standing balance following core exercises, the studies of Kadri et al. 8) and de Oliveira et al. 7) shared two commonalities: (1) the participants were healthy young 35 adults with no motor impairments, and (2) the exercise intensity was low or the duration/number of repetitions was small.
The participants were 10 males (mean age: 20.1 years, SD=0.3, CV=1.6; mean height: 171.5 cm, SD=4.6, CV=2.7; mean weight: 65.3 kg, SD=5.6, CV=8.6).
None of the participants had a history of orthopedic or neurological disorders.
During the task, participants were instructed to gaze at the anterior fixation point.
Consequently, data from 7 participants were included in the longitudinal analysis of muscle thickness.
The participants were healthy young men with relatively small variations in physical characteristics (CV=1.6-8.6).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p < 0.05", "p > 0.05", "p<0.05", 
"p<0.05"), Text = c("Results: Left-side TrA thickness during stance increased significantly under the 1-kg and 2-kg load conditions compared to baseline (p < 0.05), although substantial missing data for the left-side measurements 15 limited the robustness of this finding.", 
"No significant load-dependent effects were observed for CoP sway parameters (p > 0.05).", 
"Post-hoc 10 tests indicated that muscle thickness was significantly greater under the 1-kg and 2-kg conditions compared to baseline (p<0.05), and significantly greater under the empty box, 1-kg, and 2-kg conditions compared to body weight alone (p<0.05) (Table 1).", 
"Effects of core exercise on muscle thickness and CoP parameters across different load conditions : BL: baseline; CoP: center of pressure; SD a-p: standard deviation of CoP sway in the anteroposterior direction; SD ml: standard deviation of CoP sway in the mediolateral direction; SLS: single-leg stance; UL: upper-limb * significantly different from baseline (p<0.05, Durbin-Conover test); ** significantly different from UL elevation (upper-limb weight alone) (p<0.05, Durbin-Conover test)."
)), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p > 0.05", "p=0.11", "p=0.08", "p=0.95", "p=0.39"), Sentence = c("No significant load-dependent effects were observed for CoP sway parameters (p > 0.05).", "On the left side, the correlation was lower and non-significant (ρ=0.57, p=0.11).", "There were no significant changes in the mean velocity of CoP sway (χ2=8.24, df=4, p=0.08), mediolateral SD (χ2=0.72, 20 df=4, p=0.95), or anteroposterior SD (χ2=4.16, df=4, p=0.39).", "There were no significant changes in the mean velocity of CoP sway (χ2=8.24, df=4, p=0.08), mediolateral SD (χ2=0.72, 20 df=4, p=0.95), or anteroposterior SD (χ2=4.16, df=4, p=0.39).", "There were no significant changes in the mean velocity of CoP sway (χ2=8.24, df=4, p=0.08), mediolateral SD (χ2=0.72, 20 df=4, p=0.95), or anteroposterior SD (χ2=4.16, df=4, p=0.39)." )), row.names = c(NA, -5L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::
